title: State Management and Data Fetching
description: Where state should live and which tool fits: local, global, server, URL and form state, with Context, Redux Toolkit, Zustand, Jotai, TanStack Query, SWR, React Hook Form and Zod.

chapters.title: The Kinds of State and Where They Live
chapters.summary: Classifying state as local, shared, global, server, URL or form state, and keeping it minimal and colocated.

lesson.heading: Not all state is the same
lesson.body:
Most state management mistakes come from treating every piece of data as one kind of thing and putting it in one global store. Separate it by **who owns it** and **how it changes**:
- **Local UI state**: owned by one component. An open dropdown, a hovered row, an input draft. `useState` or `useReducer`.
- **Shared UI state**: needed by a few nearby components. Lift it to the closest common parent.
- **Global client state**: app-wide, client-owned, changes from user actions. Theme, sidebar collapsed, a shopping cart before checkout, an editor's selection. Context for low-frequency values, or a store (Zustand, Redux Toolkit, Jotai).
- **Server state**: data owned by a backend that you display a cached copy of. Users, products, orders. It can be stale, other users change it, and it needs fetching, caching, deduping and invalidation. TanStack Query, SWR, RTK Query, or framework data loading and Server Components.
- **URL state**: filters, search, pagination, selected tab. It should survive refresh and be shareable. Search params.
- **Form state**: values, validation errors, touched and dirty flags, submission status. React Hook Form or React 19 form actions.

lesson.heading: Server state is the biggest category
lesson.body:
In typical CRUD apps, most of what people put in Redux was really a cache of server data, plus hand-written `loading` and `error` flags for each request. That code is repetitive and bug-prone: no deduplication, no background refresh, stale data after mutations, race conditions.

Server-state libraries treat that data as a **cache keyed by the request**, with built-in staleness, refetching, retries and invalidation. Once server data moves there, the remaining client state is usually small enough for local state, context or a tiny store. In Next.js App Router apps, Server Components fetch much of this data on the server, shrinking client state even further.

lesson.heading: Keep state minimal: derive, do not duplicate
lesson.body:
Store the smallest set of values that can produce everything else, and compute the rest during render.
- Do not store `filteredTodos` next to `todos` and `filter`. Compute it.
- Do not store `selectedUser` as a copy; store `selectedUserId` and look it up, so edits to the user show up automatically.
- Do not mirror server data into local state with an effect; read it from the query cache.
- Replace boolean combinations with a status union: `'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'`.

Every duplicated value is a synchronization bug waiting to happen.

lesson.heading: Colocate, then lift only as needed
lesson.body:
Start state as close as possible to where it is used. Lift it only when another component needs it, and only as high as the nearest common parent. Global stores are for state that is truly global.

Colocation helps performance (updates re-render small subtrees), readability (state next to the UI that uses it) and deletion (removing a feature removes its state). A common anti-pattern is a global store holding modal open flags and form drafts for every screen.

lesson.heading: A decision guide
lesson.body:
- Comes from the server? Server-state tool (or Server Components). Not a client store.
- Should survive refresh or be shareable via link? URL search params.
- Only one component uses it? `useState`.
- A few siblings use it? Lift to the parent.
- Many distant components read it, it changes rarely? Context.
- Many components read it, it changes often, or it has complex update logic? A store with selectors.
- Is it form input? A form library or uncontrolled inputs with form actions.
- Should it persist across sessions? localStorage (via a store's persist middleware) or the server.

keyPoints: Classify state: local, shared, global client, server, URL and form.
Server state is a cache of remote data; use a server-state library or Server Components, not a global store.
Derive values during render instead of storing duplicates.
Store ids, not copies of selected objects.
Colocate state and lift only to the nearest common parent.
Use the URL for state that must survive refresh or be shared.
Reach for a global store only for truly global, frequently changing client state.

questions.prompt: A list of products loaded from an API, shown on several pages, is best classified as:
questions.explanation: The backend owns it; the client holds a cached copy that can go stale. Use a server-state tool.

questions.prompt: A product listing's category filter and page number should survive refresh and be shareable. Where should they live?
questions.explanation: URL state survives reloads, works with back/forward and can be shared as a link.

questions.prompt: What is the bug risk in this component?
options: selected holds a stale copy and does not reflect the renamed user
questions.explanation: Storing a copy duplicates data. Store selectedId and derive the user from users.

questions.prompt: Only a Tooltip component uses its isOpen flag. Where should it live?
questions.explanation: Colocate state with its only user; global placement adds coupling and unnecessary re-renders.

questions.prompt: Which state shape prevents impossible combinations?
questions.explanation: A single union cannot be loading and successful at the same time.

questions.prompt: Two sibling components both need the same counter value. What is the simplest correct approach?
options: Lift the state to their common parent and pass it down
Duplicate the state and sync with effects
questions.explanation: Lifting state to the nearest common ancestor is the default React answer for shared state.

questions.prompt: filteredItems should usually be stored in state alongside items and filter.
questions.explanation: It is derivable. Compute it during render, memoizing only if expensive.

questions.prompt: Moving server data into a server-state library often leaves very little global client state.
questions.explanation: Most global store contents in CRUD apps were server caches plus loading flags.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are good candidates for URL state?
options: Search query on a results page
questions.explanation: Shareable, refresh-surviving navigation state belongs in the URL. Sensitive and ephemeral values do not.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: data owned by a backend and cached on the client is called ___ state.
questions.explanation: Server state is remote, shared, asynchronous and can become stale.

questions.prompt: How do you decide where a piece of state should live in a React application?
questions.answer: I classify it first. If it comes from the server, it is server state and goes into TanStack Query, SWR, RTK Query or Server Components, not a hand-rolled store. If it should survive refresh or be shareable, such as filters, pagination or tabs, it goes in the URL. If it is form input, a form library or uncontrolled inputs with actions. For the rest, client UI state, I start with useState in the component that uses it, lift it to the nearest common parent when siblings need it, use context for app-wide values that change rarely (theme, current user, locale), and reach for a store with selectors (Zustand, Redux Toolkit, Jotai) when many distant components read frequently changing state or the update logic is complex. Throughout, I keep state minimal and derive everything else during render.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between server state and client state, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Client state is owned by the browser session and changes synchronously through user actions: a modal open flag, theme, a draft. It is always up to date by definition. Server state lives in a remote system: you only hold a snapshot, it is fetched asynchronously, other users or processes can change it, and it needs caching, deduplication, background refetching, retries, pagination and invalidation after mutations. Treating server state as client state (copying API responses into Redux with loading flags) means reimplementing a cache badly: stale data, waterfalls, race conditions and lots of boilerplate. Separating them lets a dedicated library handle server state, and the remaining client state becomes small and simple.

questions.prompt: What does 'derive state instead of syncing it' mean? Give an example.
questions.answer: If a value can be computed from existing props or state, compute it during render rather than storing it separately and keeping it updated with effects. Example: a todo list with todos and filter in state. Instead of a third state visibleTodos updated by a useEffect whenever todos or filter change, compute const visibleTodos = todos.filter(matches(filter)) in render, adding useMemo only if it is expensive. Storing it causes an extra render with stale data, effect bugs and inconsistency if one update path forgets to sync. Same idea for selection (store selectedId, not the object), totals in a cart, form validity, and full names from first and last.

chapters.title: Lifting State, Context and Its Limits
chapters.summary: Prop drilling, when Context is enough, why it re-renders every consumer, and the patterns that keep it fast.

lesson.heading: Prop drilling and its cheaper fixes
lesson.body:
Prop drilling is passing data through intermediate components that do not use it. A few levels are fine and keep data flow explicit. Before reaching for context, try:
- **Composition**: pass already-built elements as `children` or slot props, so the intermediate layers never see the data. `<Layout sidebar={<UserMenu user={user} />}>` means Layout does not need `user`.
- **Colocation**: move the state down to where it is used.

Context becomes the right tool when many components at different depths need the same value.

lesson.heading: Context as a transport
lesson.body:
Context does not manage state; it broadcasts a value down the tree. The state still lives in a component (`useState` or `useReducer`), and context delivers it.

A common app-level pattern is a provider component plus a custom hook that throws if used outside the provider, which gives a clear error and avoids a misleading default value.

lesson.heading: The re-render problem
lesson.body:
When a provider's `value` changes (by `Object.is`), **every** consumer re-renders, even components that only read a field that did not change. There is no selector. `React.memo` does not stop it.

Two common traps:
- An inline object `value={{ user, setUser }}` is a new reference on every provider render, so all consumers re-render whenever the provider's parent renders.
- One big `AppContext` with user, theme, cart and notifications: a new notification re-renders every component that reads the theme.

For a theme or locale that changes once per session this does not matter. For a cart that updates on every click with 200 consumers, it does.

lesson.heading: Patterns that keep context fast
lesson.body:
- **Memoize the value** with `useMemo` (or rely on React Compiler).
- **Split by concern**: separate contexts for auth, theme and cart.
- **Split state from dispatch**: put `dispatch` (stable) in one context and the state in another, so components that only trigger updates never re-render.
- **Keep fast-changing state local** or in a store.
- **Context for dependency injection**: pass a stable store or client object (a QueryClient, a Zustand store instance) through context, and let components subscribe to slices with selectors. This is how Redux, TanStack Query and per-request Zustand stores work: the context value never changes; subscriptions do the updating.

lesson.heading: When to graduate from context
lesson.body:
Move to a store when:
- many components read different slices of the same frequently changing state,
- you need selectors, devtools, middleware (persistence, logging, undo),
- state must be read or updated outside React (a WebSocket handler, a utility module),
- update logic is complex enough that you want it testable in isolation.

Zustand and Jotai are the lightweight steps; Redux Toolkit suits large teams wanting strict conventions and devtools.

keyPoints: Try composition (children, slot props) and colocation before context.
Context transports a value; the state still lives in a component.
Every consumer re-renders when the value changes; there are no selectors and memo does not help.
Memoize provider values and split contexts by concern and update frequency.
Separate state and dispatch contexts so update-only components do not re-render.
Use context to inject stable stores or clients, and subscribe with selectors.
Graduate to a store for frequent updates, many slices, middleware or access outside React.

questions.prompt: Layout passes `user` through three components that do not use it, just to reach UserMenu. Which refactor removes the drilling without context?
options: Pass <UserMenu user={user} /> as a slot prop or child to Layout
questions.explanation: Composition lets the parent build the element with the data it has, so intermediate components never see the prop.

questions.prompt: A ThemeToggle reads only setTheme from a context whose value is { theme, setTheme }. What happens when theme changes?
options: ThemeToggle re-renders because the context value changed
questions.explanation: Context has no selectors: any consumer re-renders when the value reference changes, whatever fields it reads.

questions.prompt: What does useAuth() return when called outside AuthProvider in the lesson's pattern?
questions.explanation: The default is null and the hook throws, which surfaces a missing provider immediately.

questions.prompt: Why does a memoized consumer still re-render here whenever App re-renders?
options: The value object literal is new on every render
questions.explanation: A new object reference counts as a changed value. useMemo with [user] fixes it.

questions.prompt: How do Redux and TanStack Query avoid re-rendering all components through context?
options: Context holds a stable store or client; components subscribe to specific slices with selectors
They wrap every component in memo
questions.explanation: The context value never changes. Subscriptions (via useSyncExternalStore) re-render only components whose selected data changed.

questions.prompt: Which state is a poor fit for a single app-wide context?
options: A live cursor position updated 60 times per second
questions.explanation: High-frequency updates would re-render every consumer constantly. Keep it local or in a store with selectors.

questions.prompt: dispatch from useReducer is stable, so a context that holds only dispatch never causes consumer re-renders after mount.
questions.explanation: dispatch keeps the same identity for the component's lifetime, so the context value never changes.

questions.prompt: Context is itself a state management library with selectors and middleware.
questions.explanation: Context only passes values down. State, selectors and middleware come from hooks or libraries.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: signs you should move from context to a store.
options: Many components read different slices of fast-changing state
You need to update state from a WebSocket handler outside React
You want devtools, persistence and middleware
State is used by one component
questions.explanation: Slices with frequent updates, outside-React access and middleware needs point to a store. Theme or single-component state does not.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: wrapping the provider value in ___ keeps its reference stable between renders.
questions.explanation: useMemo recreates the value object only when its dependencies change.

questions.prompt: Is React Context a replacement for Redux?
questions.answer: Partly, depending on the need. Context solves passing a value through the tree without prop drilling, and with useReducer you can build a small store. But context has no selector mechanism, so every consumer re-renders on every change, and it has no devtools, middleware, time-travel debugging or way to read and write state outside React. Redux (via Redux Toolkit) is a predictable store with selectors, devtools, middleware, conventions for large teams, and RTK Query for server state. For low-frequency app-wide values like theme, locale and auth, context is enough. For frequently changing shared state read by many components, I use a store, often Zustand for simplicity or Redux Toolkit when the team wants strict structure. And most data people used to put in Redux is server state that belongs in TanStack Query or RTK Query.

questions.prompt: How do you prevent unnecessary re-renders caused by context?
questions.answer: Memoize the provider value with useMemo (or let React Compiler do it) so it only changes when the underlying state does. Split large contexts by concern and update frequency, so a notification change does not re-render theme consumers. Put dispatch or stable callbacks in a separate context from the state they modify. Keep fast-changing values out of context entirely. Push providers down to the subtree that needs them. Use composition so expensive children are passed as children and are not re-rendered by provider state. When consumers need slices of frequently changing state, switch to a store that supports selectors, or put a stable store object in context and subscribe with useSyncExternalStore.

questions.prompt: What is prop drilling, and is it always bad?
questions.answer: Prop drilling is passing props through components that do not use them just so a deeper component can. It is not inherently bad: two or three levels keep data flow explicit, easy to trace and type-checked. It becomes a problem when many layers depend on props they ignore, making refactors painful and coupling components. Fixes in order of preference: restructure with composition (pass children or slot elements so intermediates do not need the data), colocate state closer to its users, use context for widely needed values, or a store for complex shared state. I avoid jumping to global state just to save a few props.
